summary: Describes BGMP, a protocol for inter-domain multicast routing. It builds shared trees for active multicast groups and optionally lets receiver domains build source-specific branches. The document is now historic.

eli5.summary: It was an idea for sending one message to many networks along shared tree branches. It is historic now, so it is no longer in use.

questions: how do bgmp shared trees work
how does bgmp choose a root domain
subtitle: A protocol for routing multicast data between independent networks

tldr.problem: Sending one message to many independent networks (domains) requires choosing how to build distribution trees between them, and deciding how to handle senders and receivers in different domains.
tldr.mechanism: BGMP builds shared trees rooted at domains based on multicast address ranges, optionally adds source-specific branches where needed for efficiency, and coordinates with the unicast routing protocol and intra-domain multicast protocols.
tldr.outcome: Multiple domains can efficiently exchange multicast traffic for both any-source and source-specific groups, but BGMP was experimental and is now historic, with adoption limited in favor of other approaches.

today: RFC 3913 is Historic. BGMP was an Informational protocol proposal for inter-domain multicast routing that did not become widely deployed. The inter-domain multicast architecture evolved in different directions, with SSM (source-specific multicast) becoming the primary supported mode and other approaches to inter-domain tree building adopted instead.

sections.title: Inter-Domain Multicast Routing
sections.content:
RFC 3913 describes the Border Gateway Multicast Protocol (BGMP), a protocol for routing multicast traffic between multiple independent networks (domains). Most multicast routing protocols operate within a single domain, but BGMP solves the problem of getting multicast data from a sender in one domain to receivers in other domains.

BGMP natively supports source-specific multicast (SSM), where a receiver explicitly joins a specific source address and group address pair. To also support any-source multicast (ASM), where a receiver joins a group and wants to hear from all senders, BGMP uses unicast-prefix-based multicast addressing: each domain is assigned a range of multicast addresses, and becomes the root domain for all groups in that range. BGMP uses TCP port 264 for communication between border routers, and builds trees through a series of domain-level hops rather than router-level hops.
sections.eli5: BGMP is for connecting networks that each have their own multicast system. The network where a group's addresses live becomes the root, and others connect to it. It sends messages between border routers using TCP.

sections.title: Shared Trees and Source-Specific Branches
sections.content:
BGMP builds two types of forwarding paths. A shared tree for a group is rooted at the domain that owns the group's address range. When a receiver in a domain wants to join a multicast group, its border router sends a (*,G) Join message upstream towards the root domain. This creates a shared tree through which all sources for that group send their data, like a shared meeting room that all participants enter.

A source-specific branch is an optional (S,G) tree built only where needed: when a domain wants to receive from a specific source but is not already on the shared tree, or when receiving via the shared tree would be inefficient. These branches avoid unnecessary encapsulation of data from the shared-tree ingress router to other border routers that need to inject it locally. BGMP shares these trees because most intra-domain multicast protocols (PIM-SM, DVMRP, PIM-DM) build source-specific trees internally.

A key difference from intra-domain protocols is that BGMP uses bidirectional forwarding state: packets can be forwarded to all targets in the target list without reverse-path-forwarding checks, reducing third-party dependence and allowing isolated receiver and sender domains to exchange data without relying on the root domain's connectivity.
sections.eli5: BGMP makes two kinds of paths. Shared trees are highways everyone uses to hear all senders. Source-specific branches are shortcuts when one group of networks wants one particular sender. Shared trees don't block traffic if the root has trouble.

sections.title: Design and Root Domain Selection
sections.content:
Unlike intra-domain protocols that often treat potential root candidates equally and emphasize load sharing, BGMP treats roots asymmetrically. The root domain is not random but is chosen administratively by assigning ranges of the multicast address space to domains. This gives operators fine-grained control over which domain becomes the root for any group.

This approach solves a major problem in inter-domain multicast: locality. In a domain's own part of the address space, the root is local to at least one participant (likely the session initiator), avoiding unnecessarily long paths across the Internet. The framework also supports Unicast-Prefix-Based Multicast (UPBM) addressing, where a multicast address encodes a unicast prefix that identifies the domain responsible for that group's root.
sections.eli5: Instead of randomly picking a root, BGMP lets each network own a range of group addresses. If you start a session in your network, your network becomes the root, which is more efficient.

sections.title: Interactions with Routing and Intra-Domain Protocols
sections.content:
BGMP coordinates with two other protocol systems. It interacts with the interdomain unicast routing protocol (typically BGP or MBGP) to look up routes towards sources and towards root domains. It also interacts with multicast IGPs (intra-domain multicast protocols) like PIM-SM, DVMRP, PIM-DM, CBT, and MOSPF.

When a receiver domain has PIM-SM, BGMP border routers become the ingress point for external sources and advertise themselves as Candidate Rendezvous Points (RPs). When border routers receive data packets from external sources, they check for matching (S,G) or (*,G) forwarding state. If no state exists, packets are forwarded towards the next-hop domain according to the multicast routing table. BGMP border routers also handle encapsulation of data from receiving routers to other border routers that need to inject it for RPF checks to work correctly in DVMRP and PIM-DM domains.
sections.eli5: BGMP uses the same routing tables as unicast routing to find the next network. It talks to the multicast system inside each network to know when to create paths and where to send data.

sections.title: Message Types and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
BGMP border routers communicate with each other by opening TCP connections and exchanging four message types. An OPEN message initiates a connection and confirms parameters between peers. UPDATE messages carry (*,G) and (S,G) Join and Prune notifications: Join messages create forwarding state and propagate upstream, while Prune messages remove targets from the forwarding tree. KEEPALIVE messages ensure TCP connections remain alive. NOTIFICATION messages report errors and close connections.

Join and Prune processing builds incremental state without periodic refresh: a border router receiving a Join creates forwarding state if needed and adds the requesting peer or component to its target list. If this is the first request for that entry, the router propagates the Join upstream towards the root or source. Prune messages remove requesters and propagate upstream if the target list becomes empty. Special Poison-Reverse messages prevent routing loops when a domain is on the path between source and root.
sections.eli5: Border routers open TCP connections and exchange four kinds of messages: handshakes, join/prune commands, keepalives, and error reports. Joins create paths upstream; prunes clean them up when no one is interested.
